Q: create an new app with the latest version of nextjs A:

(The working fix for the latest Next.js 16.1.6 as of Feb 27, 2026) The following steps fix this problem for me in a PNPM workspace:

⚠️ Note that Next.js automatically detects the root directory of your project. It does so by looking for one of these files: pnpm-lock.yaml, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, bun.lock, and bun.lockb (quoted from next.config.js: turbopack | Next.js).

  1. Remove all the installed modules and lockfiles with rm -rf node_modules pnpm-lock.*.yaml package-lock.json && pnpm -r exec rm -rf node_modules (or remove pnpm-lock.yaml instead if you don't use Git Branch Lockfiles | pnpm)

  2. According to the official doc Getting Started with ESLint - ESLint - Pluggable JavaScript Linter, to ensure that pnpm installs dependencies in a way that is more compatible with npm and is less likely to produce errors, be sure to create a .npmrc file with at least the following settings:

auto-install-peers=true
node-linker=hoisted

Or just add nodeLinker: hoisted to pnpm-workspace.yaml in a PNPM workspace (autoInstallPeers defaults to true)

  1. Run pnpm i

  2. Specify turbopack.root in next.config.ts as below:

import path from 'path';
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  /* config options here */
  reactCompiler: true,
  turbopack: {
    root: path.join(__dirname, '../../') // see my project structure below,
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

Below is the structure of my PNPM monorepo (the next.config.ts file is at apps/private-superapp/next.config.ts):

.
├── apps
│   ├── google-workspace-app
│   └── private-superapp (← this is a Next.js app)
│       ├── amplify

Q: How can I build a separate main.css file from src/styles that doesn't get bundled with page specific css files? A:

Yes, this is possible in Astro. The key is to stop importing main.css inside a component and instead link it as a static asset directly in your base layout.

https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/project-structure/

Move main.css to the public/ folder:

public/
  styles/
    main.css

Then in MainLayout.astro, link it with a plain <link> tag instead of an import:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles/main.css" />

And keep your page-specific styles as scoped or imported CSS as usual:

---
// aboutPage.astro
import '../styles/aboutPage.css';
---

This way main.css is served as a separate static file, cached by the browser after the first load, and never bundled into page-specific CSS files.

The HMR caveat: files in public/ are not processed by Vite, so you lose HMR on main.css. If HMR matters to you, keep it in src/ and link it differently — put it in src/styles/main.css and import it only in MainLayout.astro but via a ?url import:

https://vite.dev/guide/assets#explicit-url-imports

---
import mainCssUrl from '../styles/main.css?url';
---
<link rel="stylesheet" href={mainCssUrl} />

This tells Vite to emit it as a separate file rather than bundling it, and you keep HMR. This is the cleaner approach for your use case.

Q: How do I detect and connect to a hidden SSID on my Raspiberry Pi 3 (Raspbian)? A:

For Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm and later, the old dhcpcd-based approach stopped being the default network manager, and NetworkManager(nmcli) became the standard way to manage network connections. u confirm this by checking whether the file /etc/network/interfaces no longer exists.

To connect to a hidden Wi-Fi network, you can now do it with a single command:
sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "<ssid>" password <password> hidden yes
